description: I'm Raj, a first-year CS student just starting out. I used AI a lot to build my idea: a kids' Moon/Mars base game that uses real NASA space-weather data. It already works as a prototype. Looking for teammates who can help with: kid-friendly art and design, simple science explanations, and testing with kids. Beginners welcome!
summary: A browser game for kids ages 7–12 where you build a Moon or Mars outpost and learn why every choice costs something. Power, air and radiation shielding compete, and a real NASA DONKI solar event sets how strong the storm is.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Space education for kids often shows mission outcomes, not the trade-offs behind them. A choice that saves power today can cost oxygen tomorrow, but few tools let kids feel that.

WHAT IT IS

Outpost: Build, Run & Test is a browser game with no download or account. Players manage a lunar or Martian base for 12 days and keep two astronauts, Maya and Leo, safe.

HOW IT PLAYS

- Build: place modules (solar panels, oxygen generator, regolith walls, lab, battery) on a grid. Players get 2 builds a day, and each one spends power.

- Run: watch the day play out. Power, air and each astronaut's radiation dose change.

- Learn: see what changed and improve the base tomorrow.

- Lunar night (days 7–9) removes solar power, so players plan ahead.

- A Forecast Bench gives a rough "OK / Risky / Likely to fail" check, but it costs power and cannot predict surprises.

- Mars mode adds sols (24h 39m), dust storms and radio delay.

THE CORE TRADE-OFF

There is no free action. Power runs the base, makes air, and builds shielding. Spend it on science and you may be short on air or shielding later.

REAL NASA DATA

- NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database): the game fetches a recent coronal mass ejection (CME) and uses its speed to set the storm tier (LOW, MEDIUM or HIGH). Today's example: a CME at 530 km/s on 2026-11-15 became a MEDIUM storm.

- If the live fetch fails, the game shows "Using saved NASA data (not live)" instead of claiming live data.

- The data source is shown in the game with a "Where is this from?" link.

FOR AGES 7–12

Cadet mode (6×4 grid, ages 7–9) and Explorer mode (8×5 grid, ages 10–12). Tap "?" to get a one-line explanation of terms like Dose, CME, Sols and regolith. Mission codes and layout codes let a class replay or share the same base.

HONEST LIMITS

Module costs, the 25% wall shielding effect, the 0–100 scales and the storm-tier thresholds are simplified teaching numbers, not NASA hardware specs or official classes. This is stated in the game's "How real is this?" panel.
